title: AI, Complex Decision-Making and the Future of the Legal Profession
author: Anthea Roberts · David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source shifts the focus from commercial value capture and competition among firms, platforms, ALSPs and clients to profession-wide system dynamics. It emphasizes how AI affects expertise, organisational culture, training and law’s broader societal role, without substantively assessing pricing, buyer power, capital or changing delivery-market boundaries.
qs: We like to trace these dynamics across scales because AI is not just affecting individual lawyers — it is reshaping the system of the legal profession at every level.
The implications go well beyond what it will be like to practice law or how individual lawyers' roles will change — though both matter enormously.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability

It also sharpens the strategic interpretation of Harvey as an effort to build on law’s structural position while leaving platform capture and durable success unresolved.

kp.k: AI is restructuring a professional system, not merely tasks
kp.d: Roberts and Wilkins argue that AI is changing legal service delivery, provider identities, training and professional judgment through interacting forces that cannot be understood simply by tracking tool adoption. This is the project's organizing thesis rather than a measured finding presented in this document.
qs: It is structurally reconfiguring the profession — how legal services are delivered, who delivers them, how lawyers are trained, and what it means to exercise professional judgment.
It requires seeing the legal profession as a system — one in which multiple forces interact in ways that no single vantage point can capture.

kp.k: Integrative judgment is becoming central to legal expertise
kp.d: Drawing on Wilkins's observations of lawyers, particularly general counsel, the authors argue that high-end legal work integrates law with business, risk, strategy, politics and public relations. They contend that growing volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity make this strategic capacity increasingly central, rather than an optional complement to narrow legal expertise.
qs: The best lawyers — and particularly general counsel — don't just do legal tasks.
They operate at the intersection of law, business, risk, strategy, politics, and public relations.

But as the world has become more volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous — what strategists call a VUCA world — this integrative capacity has moved from a nice-to-have to the core of what the profession needs.

kp.k: Dragonfly thinking supplies a multi-perspective decision framework
kp.d: The authors connect Wilkins's account of effective lawyering with Roberts's dragonfly thinking methodology: integrating diverse perspectives and competing arguments to navigate complexity. They attribute the framework's forecasting foundation to Philip Tetlock's research, but provide no study details or quantitative results here.
qs: What Anthea calls "dragonfly thinking" draws on Philip Tetlock's research on expert forecasting, which found that the best forecasters aren't deep specialists but integrative thinkers who see through multiple lenses simultaneously.
Dragonfly thinking, as a methodology, involves synthesizing a multitude of points, counterpoints, and counter-counterpoints so that the integrated whole is more valuable than the sum of its parts.

kp.k: AI agents could augment complex human decision-making
kp.d: The authors describe agents developed through Roberts's start-up as tools for multi-lens risk, strategy and policy analysis, not specifically legal AI tools. Their intended role is human augmentation: mapping actors, tracing drivers, exploring scenarios, challenging assumptions and helping interdisciplinary teams align. A 2024 Harvard workshop with chief legal officers and managing partners provided demonstrations and interaction, not a reported controlled evaluation of effectiveness.
qs: These aren't legal AI tools.

They're a method for AI-enabled multi-lens analysis across risk, strategy and policy — systems that help leaders map actors, trace drivers, run scenarios, challenge their own assumptions, and surface blind spots they didn't know they had.
The tools operationalize the dragonfly thinking methodology: they help humans hold more perspectives and system dynamics in mind than unaided cognition allows.

In 2024, we co-led a [senior leadership workshop](https://clp.law.harvard.edu/knowledge-hub/insights/senior-leadership-workshop-on-dragonfly-thinking/) at Harvard with chief legal officers from Blackstone, Vanguard, BlackRock, and AIG, and managing partners from Morgan Lewis, Orrick, and McGuireWoods.

kp.k: Hands-on AI use exposes the importance of domain expertise
kp.d: The authors report using Dragonfly agents to analyze AI's professional impact and co-create papers and visualizations. Their firsthand experience includes both unexpected insights and fluent nonsense detectable only by experts. This supports their emphasis on domain expertise but supplies no measured error rates or systematic performance comparison.
qs: We are using AI tools to analyze AI's impact on the profession and we will be sharing a series of papers and visualizations we have co-created with various Dragonfly agents.

We're living it from the inside — experiencing firsthand the gap between model capability and domain expertise, the moments when AI surfaces something genuinely surprising and the moments when it produces fluent nonsense that only an expert would catch.

kp.k: Individual adaptation affects firm competition and professional expertise
kp.d: The authors report anxiety among students and senior lawyers about the future value of qualifications and expertise, alongside differing willingness to learn AI tools. They propose a cross-scale mechanism: individual resistance shapes practice culture, delayed firm adoption changes competitive positioning, and inadequate training threatens the expertise underpinning professional authority. These are qualitative observations and risk arguments, not quantified labor-market findings.
qs: They're responses to genuine uncertainty about what expertise means when machines can do things that used to require years of training.
A partner who resists learning AI shapes a practice group's culture.
A firm that delays adoption shifts its competitive position.
A profession that underinvests in training its next generation risks hollowing out the expertise on which its authority rests.

kp.k: Law's centrality creates opportunities for platform capture
kp.d: The authors argue that law's connections across business and society make it a strategic entry point for AI into professional services. They frame the consequences for market participants, law-firm business models and hourly billing as open questions, especially whether lawyers retain the value of this central position or platforms capture it. Their summary of the gateway essay presents this as a strategic argument, not an established market outcome.
qs: They extend to the business model of law firms, which players are in the market, the future of the billable hour, and whether law's structural centrality holds, expands, or gets captured by the platforms being built on top of it.

**Law is the gateway drug** argues that law's structural position — at the center of business, connecting every other function — makes it the natural entry point for AI across all professional services.
The question: does law capture the gateway position, or does the gateway capture law?

kp.k: Harvey is framed as a strategic platform-building actor
kp.d: The document describes Roberts reading Harvey's $11 billion valuation as a technology strategy play and previews an essay arguing that the company should not be understood merely as a ChatGPT wrapper. It positions Harvey as attempting to build on law's structural centrality, without supplying detailed evidence of its strategy in this overview.
qs: She follows AI developments closely and reads market moves like Harvey's $11 billion valuation as technology strategy plays.
**Harvey's Strategic Evolution** examines what the most-discussed legal AI company actually appears to be building — and why reading it as a "ChatGPT wrapper" misses the strategic thesis entirely.
Harvey's Strategic Evolution shows a company trying to build on that structural position.

kp.k: Automation may undermine the pathway to elite legal expertise
kp.d: The authors preview further work on competitive change, training and a proposed shift from up-or-out to up-and-out. The training concern is framed as a question about whether elite lawyering remains attainable if AI automates the staffing pyramid's base and erodes the developmental ladder. The document does not explain the proposed career-system variant or enumerate the announced four ingredients of good AI outcomes.
qs: **The Scrambled Competitive Map** (the competitive landscape AI is redrawing — incumbents, challengers, and clients all exerting gravitational pull)
**The Training Crisis** (the four ingredients of good AI outcomes, and why the profession is systematically undermining the scarcest one)
**From Up or Out to Up and Out** (where elite lawyering goes when AI automates the base of the pyramid — and whether the destination is reachable when the ladder behind it is collapsing)

kp.k: Evidence is differentiated, triangulated and treated as provisional
kp.d: The authors describe a first-release corpus of 170 sources across 39 topics in 11 dimensions, subsequently expanded for three flagship papers. Sources are coded against claims they support, complicate or distinguish. Scholarship, legal materials, industry evidence and interviews serve different evidentiary functions; vendor statements, valuations, forecasts and podcasts are not treated as standalone proof. The authors explicitly present their analysis as evolving frameworks rather than settled predictions.
qs: The topic network visualization maps the first-release corpus behind this project — 170 sources across 39 topics in 11 dimensions, from market dynamics and technology evolution to competitive dynamics, human-AI collaboration, and professional identity.
Each source is coded against the claims it supports, complicates, or distinguishes, so the papers rest on a source map rather than a generic literature review.
We do not treat vendor claims, funding-round valuations, consultancy forecasts, or podcast statements as freestanding proof.
They are triangulated against the broader corpus and labelled for what they are.
We're interested less in predicting who wins than in helping people see the system clearly enough to make better decisions within it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts and Wilkins describe AI as a structural transformation of legal services, rather than merely another tool adoption cycle.
pts.d: The authors claim that AI is already changing service delivery, who provides legal services, training, and professional judgment. They extend the implications to law-firm business models, market participants, and hourly billing, but do not specify a particular outcome for the billable hour. Whether law's central position expands or is captured by platforms is presented as an open question, not a settled prediction.

pts.k: AI agents may augment complex, high-end judgment by expanding the perspectives decision-makers can consider.
pts.d: Roberts and Wilkins distinguish this augmentation thesis from routine-task automation. They describe Roberts's Dragonfly Thinking agents as designed to map actors, trace drivers, explore scenarios, challenge assumptions, and expose blind spots across risk, strategy, and policy. These are explicitly not legal-specific tools, although the authors have introduced them to legal leaders. Improvement in complex decision-making is framed as a possibility and design objective, rather than a measured performance finding.

pts.k: Expertise remains important because useful AI insights coexist with convincing errors that require an expert to detect.
pts.d: The authors report this from their own use of AI agents to research and write about the profession. Their account supports a human-in-the-loop model: model capability alone does not ensure sound domain-specific results. The document does not supply error rates or a formal verification protocol.

pts.k: Individual adoption choices and training investment have consequences for firms' competitiveness and the profession's expertise.
pts.d: Roberts and Wilkins argue that resistance to learning AI can shape practice-group culture, delayed firm adoption changes competitive positioning, and inadequate investment in the next generation risks weakening the expertise supporting professional authority. Their previews of forthcoming essays go further, positing automation of junior work and a threatened development ladder. Those previews do not establish the scale of automation or explain the proposed 'up and out' model.

pts.k: Law's connections across business make it a potential entry point for AI into other professional services, with platforms competing to capture that position.
pts.d: Summarizing their opening essays, Roberts and Wilkins argue that law's structural centrality makes it a natural gateway for AI across professional services and helps explain capital inflows. They interpret Harvey, the legal-AI company, as trying to build on that position rather than merely wrapping a chatbot. They also signal a changing competitive landscape involving incumbents, challengers, and clients, without predicting a winner or supplying detailed market-share forecasts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The immediate basis is professional research experience, hands-on AI use, and engagement with legal leaders, rather than quantified causal evidence.
pts.d: The authors invoke Wilkins's decades studying legal institutions and Roberts's experience building and orchestrating AI tools. They describe a 2024 Harvard workshop involving chief legal officers and managing partners, subsequent practitioner conversations, teaching, and an April 2026 colloquium. These establish experience and opportunities to test frameworks; the document reports no controlled assessment of improved legal judgment, productivity, employment, or client outcomes. Roberts's role as founder of the tool-building startup is disclosed. Tetlock's forecasting research is cited as an intellectual basis for integrating perspectives, not as a direct test of these AI tools.

pts.k: The project reports a broad, expanding source corpus, while explicitly treating market and participant statements as signals requiring triangulation.
pts.d: The authors report an initial corpus of 170 sources spanning 39 topics and 11 dimensions, subsequently expanded to include scholarship, legal materials, market records, investor materials, and interviews. This document describes the sourcing method rather than presenting claim-specific empirical results from that corpus. Harvey's reported $11 billion valuation is used as a strategic market signal, not proof of capability or future success.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Structural change is described as underway in 2026 and continuing for years, with no quantified adoption or displacement timetable.
pts.d: The authors present current reconfiguration alongside conditional futures. Better complex decision-making depends on effective human use of agents and domain expertise; weakened professional expertise is a risk where training is underfunded; the career-ladder concern is linked to automation at the pyramid's base. Platform capture and competitive winners remain unresolved. The authors repeatedly characterize the work as evolving frameworks rather than final predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims span senior decision-makers, junior lawyers, firms, clients, legal education, and AI platforms, with particular attention to corporate and elite practice.
pts.d: General counsel and senior partners are potential users of AI-assisted strategic judgment. Students and junior lawyers face uncertainty about credentials and the acquisition of expertise as foundational work is automated; senior lawyers face adaptation demands and concerns about the value of accumulated expertise. Practice groups and firms face cultural, competitive, and business-model changes. Clients, incumbent providers, challengers, and platforms participate in the redrawn market, while educators face training responsibilities. Student fears about worthless degrees are reported anxieties, not an author prediction that degrees will become worthless. The document does not provide a specific claim about access to justice or quantify effects on the public.
